seo.title: Karmic tail 21 16 4 compatibility: The World, The Tower, The Emperor
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 16 4 compatibility: what The World, The Tower and The Emperor mean for a couple, how it is worked out, and why its happy ending comes first.

title: Karmic tail 21-16-4 in compatibility: the couple whose ending comes first
short: The couple's karmic tail 21-16-4 begins with The World — the card of completion, the "final message" of the Major Arcana — and ends with The Emperor, one of the first cards in the row. It runs backwards: first "happily ever after", then the foundation that such happiness rests on. The couple enters the task feeling that they already have everything, lives through the collapse of that feeling, and learns the main thing: how to build a shared order in which both of them have a voice.

sections.h2: How the 21-16-4 tail is calculated: an example with two dates
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices; if the sum is above 22, its digits are added together. Take the dates 05.12.1976 and 14.09.1975. The first partner's personal tail is 3-7-22, the second's is 18-9-9. Add top to top, middle to middle, bottom to bottom:

Here is the first oddity. Add the two ends of the tail, 21 + 4 = 25 → 7, and you would get The Chariot. But a couple's middle is not derived from the ends: it is the sum of the partners' middles, 7 + 9. With these two ends, the personal formula could never produce a sixteen in the middle.

The whole 21-16-4 tail is impossible for one person, too. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, so to have The World on top with a four at the bottom, the centre would have to be The Star, 17. No birth date puts The Star in the centre of a personal matrix. A couple's matrix can hold it: our partners' centres are 8 and 9, which make 17. Both this tail and this Star exist only for two.

About one couple in 137 has 21-16-4 — 48th place among the 97 couple tails. It is put together in two ways: from the personal tails 18-9-9 and 3-7-22, as in our example (71.5% of such couples), or from 15-8-11 and 6-8-20 (28.5%). No couple tail uses the same numbers in another order: a search through every date produced neither 21-4-16 nor any order with 16 or 4 in front.

sections.h2: A romance that begins with the wedding
paragraphs: Around 1170 Chrétien de Troyes wrote "Erec and Enide", one of the earliest Arthurian romances. In the prologue he boasts that he has drawn from "a tale of adventure" une mout bele conjointure — "a most beautiful joining". The word means a skilfully assembled plot, but literally it is a "joining together", parts fitted into a whole. A couple's matrix is built the same way: two matrices added into a third.

The romance is built in an unusual way. The knight Erec, son of King Lac, meets a poor girl in an old dress, wins the prize for the fairest lady for her in single combat and brings her to Arthur's court. The wedding comes at about line two thousand out of nearly seven thousand: where a fairy tale puts a full stop, Chrétien is only starting. The reader does not even learn the bride's name until the altar, because "a wife is not wed unless she is called by her rightful name". Her name is Enide. Everything else is about what happens after "happily ever after".

The 21-16-4 tail is built the same way: the final card stands at the entrance. The three acts of the romance fall on the three cards in order. This is our reading, not Chrétien's design, but there are too many matches to walk past. The quotations below are our own translations from the Old French.

After the wedding Erec takes Enide to his father's town of Carnant, which has everything: forests and meadows, vineyards, orchards and rivers. He loves his wife so much that he gives up tournaments and arms, and often gets up when it is already past noon. He still hands out horses and armour to his knights generously, but he himself goes nowhere. The world shrinks to one room, and in that room nothing is lacking.

From outside, this world looks different. The court whispers that Erec has turned recreant — a knight who has given up, a coward — and Enide gets the blame: she has supposedly ensnared him. Enide hears all of it and says nothing, because her husband would take offence if she spoke. One morning, while he sleeps, her tears break through, and with them a short sentence: "Con mar i fus!" — "Ill-fated you are!" Erec is only dozing, and he hears.

Getting ready for the road, Enide names the loss herself: "I was too much at ease: there was nothing I lacked." It is worth remembering that "nothing I lacked", in Old French ne me faloit nule chose. It comes back in the last scene of the romance.

This is what The World looks like at the entry to the tail. What a 21-16-4 couple wants together is a full, finished world for two. In its bright form this means freedom, a shared outlook, the open road. In its shadow it means closedness and secrets. It can go like this: the two are happy together, meetings with friends are cancelled one after another, relatives tell one of the partners "you two have vanished" — and that partner does not pass it on, so as not to spoil things. The world is full, except that everything said about it from outside piles up inside one of the two. That is why the entry to the task so easily becomes resistance: the more perfect the world for two, the more frightening it is to change anything in it.

Among the wedding guests, by the way, is the lord of the Isle of Glass, where "no thunder is heard, no lightning falls and there is no storm". The World this tail begins with is exactly that kind of country. There is no Tower in it yet.

sections.h2: The Tower: she rides ahead and keeps silent
paragraphs: Erec does not argue. "You were right," he says, "and those who blame me are right." And at once he tells her to get up, put on her finest dress and saddle her best horse. He arms himself, refuses an escort — only his wife will go with him — and leads her off, in Chrétien's words, "not knowing where, at a venture". On the road he gives an order that alone is worth rereading the romance for:
"Take care not to be so bold that, whatever you may see, you tell me of it. Do not speak to me unless I address you first. Ride ahead, and fast."

"She went ahead and fell silent. Neither said a word to the other." Enide whispers to herself: "To such great joy had God raised me up — and in a short hour He has cast me down." This is The Tower in a single line: the height you fall from and the short hour of the fall.

Chrétien never says why Erec does this. In the Welsh retelling of the same story, "Geraint son of Erbin", the husband suspects his wife of loving another man and makes her wear her worst dress. In Chrétien there is no jealousy and no rival, and the dress is the finest. What collapses is not fidelity but two invented images. Erec, "the best knight in the world", learns how others see him. Enide, who "lacked for nothing", learns that her happiness is called his disgrace. And suddenly each sees the other as a stranger: on the road Erec will throw at her that he "knew very well all along that you hardly value me at all".

Lisovskaya describes The Tower among a couple's tasks in almost the same picture: the invented image of the partner collapses, hard events come one after another, and in trouble the two look in different directions. In Chrétien it is not a metaphor. Enide rides in front, Erec behind, and she is forbidden even to turn round.

Then come blow after blow: three robbers, then five, a count who wants to take Erec's wife from him, two giants. Again and again Enide sees the danger first and has to choose between the ban and her husband. "He will kill me. Let him kill me! I will not keep silent — I will tell him." Erec wins and scolds her every time: next time I will not forgive you. The voice that saves him is punished for having spoken.

In a modern couple, the middle of 21-16-4 can look entirely ordinary. After a hard conversation the two live "in business mode": they sort things out, pay the bills, drive the children around — and barely talk. One of them, like Enide, is the first to notice what is coming and decides each time whether to break the silence. The other, like Erec, copes alone and is annoyed at being warned. Difficulties come in a row, and the two go through them not hand in hand, but one after the other.

Here the numbers of the tail drop a clue. In 71.5% of couples with this tail, The Tower is made of 7 and 9 — The Chariot and The Hermit, the road and solitude. That is exactly what Chrétien wrote: a ride without words. In the other 28.5% the middle is 8 + 8, two Justices. And the line with which Erec gets out of bed is about two rights: in "you were right, and those who blame me are right" the Old French uses droit both times — "right, being in the right". The road begins with a double verdict.

The turning point comes at Limors. Badly wounded, Erec collapses senseless and is taken for dead. Count Oringle carries the body and Enide to his castle and that same evening marries her against her will. She refuses to eat; the count strikes her and speaks a formula in which the shadow of The Emperor shows without disguise: "The lady is mine and I am hers, and I will do with her as I please." Enide answers that she fears neither his blows nor his threats.

At that moment Erec comes to — "when he heard his wife's voice". The voice that was forbidden to speak brings him back to life. The guests flee shouting "Run, run, the dead man!", and Erec puts Enide in front of him on a single horse. "The horse carries them both." A moment ago they rode apart, she in front and he behind. Now they share one saddle.

That same night he tells her: "Sweet sister, I have tested you to the full. Now I love you more than ever before, and I know that you love me with a perfect love. From now on I am wholly at your command, as I used to be." It is easy to decide here that the way out is simply to change who gives the orders. The romance does not end like that: the garden and the two crowns are still ahead.

Here, too, the numbers know more than it seems. In 28.5% of couples with this tail, The Emperor is made of 11 and 20 — Strength and Judgement. Strength is Enide facing the count; Judgement is the card of waking and of the call: Erec rises at the call of a voice. In 71.5% of couples The Emperor is the sum of 22 and 9, The Fool and The Hermit: the road taken "at a venture" and the decision to ride without an escort. Partners with the tails 18-9-9 and 3-7-22 have no Emperor either in the personal tail or in the centre: it is born only in the sum. In the pairing of 15-8-11 and 6-8-20 it is the other way round: both partners carry The Emperor in the centre of their personal matrix, and in the couple's centre 4 + 4 gives Justice — two rulers and a pair of scales between them.

sections.h2: The Emperor: two crowns and a robe on which the world is measured
paragraphs: The last scene of the romance is Christmas at Nantes. Erec's father dies, and Arthur crowns the new couple. Two crowns of fine gold are brought out: two maidens hold one, two knights the other. The bishop anoints Erec, and Arthur puts in his hand a sceptre of solid emerald on which every fish, beast, man and bird in the world is carved. Then Enide receives her crown. The woman who was forbidden to speak is crowned beside her husband.

Erec wears a robe embroidered by four fairies. The first portrayed Geometry — how she measures "how far the heavens and the earth extend, so that nothing is lacking", and so "measures the whole world". The second portrayed Arithmetic, who counts the days and hours, the drops of the sea, the grains of sand and the stars: "numbers never deceived her". The third embroidered Music, the fourth Astronomy.

Here is the promised return. "So that nothing is lacking" on the robe — de rien nule n'i faut — uses the same verb as Enide's morning lament: ne me faloit nule chose. In bed, the fullness of the world was given as a gift and measured by nothing. On the king's robe it is measured: height, width, depth, number. The World from the entry of the tail comes back at the end, but now as measure. **In the 21-16-4 tail The Emperor does not cancel happiness: he draws its plan.**

The romance shows The Emperor in shadow twice, and both forms are easy to recognise. First the empty throne: a king's son who does not rule, does not ride out and decides nothing, while gossip rules in his place. Then the decree: "do not speak unless I address you". Enide breaks it again and again, each time for her husband's sake. It is a rule that later gets in its own author's way: he has to forgive his wife for saving him. And Erec has no face that shows what he feels — all along the road Enide wonders whether this is anger or a test.

The couple's main task is to turn "we have everything" into "we have it all worked out". Who decides about money and who about holidays. How much time belongs to each partner's friends. What to do if one of them hears something unpleasant about the couple. Which rules are shared, and which have long been in the way and survive only out of habit. This is The Emperor's order in a couple: not a throne for one and not a decree, but a structure the two have agreed on out loud.

sections.h2: The garden behind a wall of air
paragraphs: Before the coronation Chrétien places an episode that feels like a dream. The castle of Brandigan is so strong that it "fears neither king nor emperor". By the castle lies a garden with no wall and no fence around it, only air, yet the enchanted air holds as if the garden were closed in iron. Flowers and ripe fruit grow there all year round. The fruit may be eaten inside, but whoever tries to carry even one piece out will not find the way out until he puts it back in its place.

A couple lives in the garden. The knight Mabonagrain once promised his beloved to grant her a request — "I pledged my word to her, and did not know to what". She demanded that he never leave the garden until someone defeated him in combat. He stayed, and did not let her see how hard it was for him: he was afraid she would take back her heart. They had left her home in secret, "so that no one knew of it but the two of us". When Enide and the lady recognise each other as cousins, Enide tells her own story differently: she was given in marriage so that "my father knew, and my mother rejoiced".

Erec defeats Mabonagrain and blows the horn that no one before him could sound. The captive is free, and the celebration is called "the Joy of the Court": the joy of two becomes the joy of all. This is the mirror of the 21-16-4 tail — a World the couple never left. A perfect garden, a secret union, a vow made blind, displeasure hidden out of love — and strangers pay for this closed harmony: in the garden stand stakes with the helmets of the defeated. The tail shows what happens if a couple stays at the entrance for ever.

One more clue is "The couple's values", the spiritual purpose. In 69% of couples with this tail it holds The Lovers, the card of choice; in 31%, The Devil, the card of a bond that holds. In our example it is The Devil. For couples with The Devil, Mabonagrain's garden is a warning about a bond held by a vow rather than by desire. For couples with The Lovers, it is a reminder that a choice is not made only once. Erec and Enide leave their Tower precisely by choosing: she chooses to speak, he chooses to listen.

sections.h2: What Waite says: a song at the laying of a stone
paragraphs: Having called The World "this final message of the Major Trumps", Waite adds that it is "perhaps more especially a story of the past, referring to that day when all was declared to be good, when the morning stars sang together and all the Sons of God shouted for joy". The words come from the Book of Job (38:7), and the verses before them are worth reading: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?.. Who hath laid the measures thereof?.. Whereupon are the foundations thereof fastened? or who laid the corner stone thereof". The joy with which Waite explains The World is the joy at the laying of a stone.

Waite's Emperor "is executive and realization", and the author notes that "he is occasionally represented as seated on a cubic stone". So the first and last cards of the tail are already linked in Waite's own text: the song of The World rings out over The Emperor's stone. A 21-16-4 couple hears the song before laying the stone. The likeness to Erec's robe, embroidered with measure, number, music and stars, is our observation, not Chrétien's intent: the four arts were the standard set of medieval learning. But next to Job it rings true.

In his list of divinatory meanings Waite calls The Tower "a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe". And in the centre of 71.5% of such couples stands The Star — the card that follows The Tower in the deck. Waite's figure on it pours "on the waters of the soul some part and measure of her priceless possession". The atmosphere inside this couple is what comes after the lightning: not armour, but water. In Chrétien, once the danger is past, Enide takes Erec's armour off, washes and binds his wounds, and lets no one else touch him. In the other 28.5% of couples the centre holds Justice — the scales on which the two weigh their rights.

sections.h2: How a couple steps out of the 21-16-4 script
paragraphs: The romance gives no recipe, but it shows exactly where things break and where they mend. Here is what follows from it for two people.

ul: **Say by day what is heard at night.** Enide kept the gossip to herself until it broke out one morning in bed, through tears, over her sleeping husband. Other people's words about the couple — from relatives, friends, colleagues — are better brought into the conversation while they are still news, not a verdict.

**Do not answer pain with a decree.** "Don't speak to me" is the natural reaction of someone who has been hurt. But rules like that later have to be broken for the sake of the very person who made them. If the urge is to forbid, it is more honest to say that it hurts.
**Ride side by side after the blow.** Troubles are not split into "yours" and "mine". In a hard period, decide together and out loud, even if one of the two has more strength right now.

**Measure your world.** Translate "we have everything" into agreements: money, home, time for oneself and for friends, who is responsible for what. And revise them when life changes: a rule that is never revised turns into a garden behind a wall of air.

**Two crowns, not one.** Order does not mean that one gives orders and the other obeys, nor that the two swap roles. Each has an area where they decide, and there are shared questions where both decide.
**Let people into the garden.** Friends, family and shared projects with other people keep a world for two from becoming an enchanted garden.

paragraphs: If in a real couple one partner forbids the other to speak, threatens them or raises a hand, this is not "a lesson of The Emperor" but danger. What is needed here is help from people: a local emergency number, a crisis line, a psychologist.

sections.h2: The strong version of the couple's 21-16-4 tail
paragraphs: The strong version of this couple is two people who have been through their Tower and know each other's voice. Their order was not invented by one of them: it was measured by both, like Erec's robe. Their world is not closed — others are glad of it too, as of "the Joy of the Court". Lisovskaya writes that many see a couple with The World in its bright form as ideal. For 21-16-4 this is not a shop window at the start but the result: an ideal that was built, not given.

After "the Joy of the Court" Chrétien slips in a line that is easy to miss: "Nor was Enide mute as she took leave of the barons: she greeted them all by name." The girl with no name until her wedding, the wife who was forbidden to speak, now calls every person by name. That is the whole road of the 21-16-4 tail: **from a world that needs no words to an order in which everyone has a voice.**

ul: **Entry to the task — 21, The World.** What the couple wants together: a whole world for two, full and finished, with nothing left to add. It is also the resistance: a world like that easily closes itself off from everyone else.

**Middle of the task — 16, The Tower.** The road runs through the collapse of invented images — of oneself and of the partner. What was left unsaid breaks out, and for a while the two travel in silence, one behind the other rather than side by side.
**Main task — 4, The Emperor.** To build how the union works: agreements instead of orders, rules that both of them made, and a voice for each.

intro: This plot has a twin in literature, and it is more than eight centuries old. What follows is an investigation: what is written in the three cards, in the numbers of the couple's matrix, and in an old romance that begins where fairy tales end.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 21-16-4 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of a couple who begin with a sense of a finished, complete world for two (The World, 21), live through the collapse of invented images of themselves and of each other (The Tower, 16) and learn the main thing — to build a shared order with agreements and a voice for both (The Emperor, 4). The main point is The Emperor: that is where the couple has the most work to do.

faq.q: Can 21-16-4 appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and for The World over a four at the bottom the centre would have to be The Star, 17. No birth date gives a person that centre, so 21-16-4 occurs only in a couple's matrix.

faq.q: Why is the middle 16 and not 7?
faq.a: A couple's middle is not recalculated from the ends; it is the sum of the middles of the two personal tails: 7 + 9 or 8 + 8. Adding the ends, 21 + 4, would give 7, but the couple takes its middle straight from the partners, and the result is The Tower.

faq.q: Does the 21-16-4 tail predict a crisis or a break-up?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events or dates. The Tower in the middle describes how the couple travels towards its task: through a change in how they see themselves and each other, not through an appointed catastrophe. How that road goes depends on whether the two talk to each other.

faq.q: What is in the centre for couples with the 21-16-4 tail?
faq.a: In 71.5% of these couples the centre is The Star, 17 — a card that never appears in the centre of a personal matrix. In the other 28.5% the centre is Justice, 8: this happens when the tail is built from the personal tails 15-8-11 and 6-8-20.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. A search through every date produces neither 21-4-16 nor any order with 16 or 4 in front. A tail of The World, The Tower and The Emperor appears in a couple only in the order 21-16-4.
